title: Every heartbeat starts in a tiny strip of muscle that fires by itself
body: Your heart sets its own rhythm. Each beat begins in the **sinoatrial node**, a strip of specialised muscle about 15 mm long in the wall of the right atrium, whose cells never settle at rest: their voltage creeps up by itself until it fires. The pulse spreads across the atria, waits briefly at the AV node so the ventricles can fill, then races down the bundle of His and the Purkinje fibres, and the ventricles squeeze from the bottom up. Nerves only speed the pacemaker up or slow it down.

cover.alt: A large painted anatomical model of a human heart, cut open to show its thick muscle walls, valves and blood vessels

slides.alt: Animated diagram of a heart on a dark background. A spark at the sinoatrial node spreads across the atria, pauses at the AV node, then glows down the bundle of His and the Purkinje fibres into the ventricles, while an ECG trace draws the P wave, the pause, the QRS spike and the T wave in step.

slides.prompt: Speed the pacemaker up and slow it down, watching the spark, the pause at the AV node and the ECG. Then stop the SA node.
slides.takeaway: Each beat starts at the SA node and pauses at the AV node before the ventricles fire: the P wave, then the QRS. When the node stops, slower cells further down take over, here at 45 a minute, with no P waves.

slides.heading: Why the pause?
slides.text: The atria and the ventricles are electrically insulated from each other everywhere except the AV node, which holds the signal back for a moment. That lets the atria empty into the ventricles first. If both squeezed at once, the ventricles would fill poorly and blood would be pushed backwards.

slides.heading: Match each part of the ECG
slides.explanation: An ECG records the heart's electrical activity. Each bump or flat stretch is one stage of the same beat, always in this order.

slides.alt: A pink-stained microscope slide of heart tissue showing muscle fibres, pale fat cells and a small artery cut across
slides.caption: The sinoatrial node under a microscope, stained pink. Its pacemaker cells are a kind of heart muscle cell, specialised to fire on their own.

slides.heading: Found while the boss went cycling
slides.text: In a makeshift laboratory in a Kent farmhouse, the young medical student Martin Flack spotted the node in the heart of a mole while his mentor, Sir Arthur Keith, was out on a bicycle ride with his wife. They published the discovery in 1907, and it is still also called the Keith–Flack node.

left.label: Speeding up
left.text: Sympathetic nerves raise a signalling molecule called cAMP in the cells, which makes each slow voltage climb faster.

right.label: Slowing down
right.text: The vagus nerve releases acetylcholine onto the node, slowing the pacemaker and lowering the heart rate.

slides.question: If the sinoatrial node stops working, what normally takes over?
slides.explanation: Other heart cells can also start beats, just at a slower rate. Normally the node outpaces them, but if it fails, a group of cells further down becomes the pacemaker.
